books.title: Vishnu Purana
books.edition: H. H. Wilson, 1840 · six books, 126 chapters
books.accessNote: All 126 chapter headings and their PDF locations are indexed. Chapter headings are the translator’s summaries; they do not mean every passage has been reviewed or entered on the timeline.

sections.title: Book I, chapter I
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Invocation. Maitreya inquires of his teacher, Paráśara, the origin and nature of the universe. Paráśara performs a rite to destroy the demons: reproved by Vaśisht ha, he desists: Pulastya appears, and bestows upon him divine knowledge: he repeats the Vishńu Puráńa. Vishńu the origin, existence, and end of all things.

sections.title: Book I, chapter II
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Prayer of Paráśara to Vishńu. Successive narration of the Vishńu Puráńa. Explanation of Vásudeva: his existence before creation: his first manifestations. Description of Pradhána or the chief principle of things. Cosmogony. Of Prákrita, or material creation; of time; of the active cause. Developement of effects; Mahat; Ahankára; Tanmátras; elements; objects of sense; senses; of the mundane egg. Vishńu the same as Brahmá the creator; Vishńu the preserver; Rudra the destroyer.

sections.title: Book I, chapter III
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Measure of time. Moments or Kásht hás, &c.; day and night; fortnight, month, year, divine year: Yugas, or ages: Maháyuga, or great age: day of Brahmá: periods of the Manus: a Manwantara: night of Brahmá, and destruction of the world: a year of Brahmá: his life: a Kalpa: a Parárrdha: the past, or Pádma Kalpa: the present, or Váráha.

sections.title: Book I, chapter IV
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Náráyańa's appearance, in the beginning of the Kalpa, as the Varsha or boar: Prithiví (Earth) addresses him: he raises the world from beneath the waters: hymned by Sanandana and the Yogis. The earth floats on the ocean: divided into seven zones. The lower spheres of the universe restored. Creation renewed.

sections.title: Book I, chapter V
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Vishńu as Brahmá creates the world. General characteristics of creation. Brahmá meditates, and gives origin to, immovable things, animals, gods, men. Specific creation of nine kinds; Mahat, Tanmátra, Aindríya, inanimate objects, animals, gods, men, Anugraha, and Kaumára. More particular account of creation. Origin of different orders of beings from Brahmá's body under different conditions; and of the Vedas from his mouths. All things created again as they existed in a former Kalpa.

sections.title: Book I, chapter VI
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Origin of the four castes: their primitive state. Progress of society. Different kinds of grain. Efficacy of sacrifice. Duties of men: regions assigned them after death.

sections.title: Book I, chapter VII
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Creation continued. Production of the mind-born sons of Brahmá; of the Prajápatis; of Sanandana and others; of Rudra and the eleven Rudras; of the Manu Swáyambhuva, and his wife Śatarúpá; of their children. The daughters of Daksha, and their marriage to Dharma and others. The progeny of Disarms and Adharma. The perpetual succession of worlds, and different modes of mundane dissolution.

sections.title: Book I, chapter VIII
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Origin of Rudra: his becoming eight Rudras: their wives and children. The posterity of Bhrigu. Account of Śrí in conjunction with Vishńu. Sacrifice of Daksha.

sections.title: Book I, chapter IX
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Legend of Lakshmí. Durvásas gives a garland to Indra: he treats it disrespectfully, and is cursed by the Muni. The power of the gods impaired: they are oppressed by the Dánavas, and have recourse to Vishńu. The churning of the ocean. Praises of Śrí.

sections.title: Book I, chapter X
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: The descendants of the daughters of Daksha married to the Rishis.

sections.title: Book I, chapter XI
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Legend of Dhruva, the son of Uttánapáda: he is unkindly treated by his father's second wife: applies to his mother: her advice: he resolves to engage in religious exercises: sees the seven Rishis, who recommend him to propitiate Vishńu.

sections.title: Book I, chapter XII
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Dhruva commences a course of religious austerities. Unsuccessful attempts of Indra and his ministers to distract Dhruva's attention: they appeal to Vishńu, who allays their fears, and appears to Dhruva. Dhruva praises Vishńu, and is raised to the skies as the pole-star.

sections.title: Book I, chapter XIII
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Posterity of Dhruva. Legend of Veńa: his impiety: he is put to death by the Rishis. Anarchy ensues. The production of Nisháda and Prithu: the latter the first king. The origin of Súta and Mágadha: they enumerate the duties of kings. Prithu compels Earth to acknowledge his authority: he levels it: introduces cultivation: erects cities. Earth called after him Prithiví: typified as a cow.

sections.title: Book I, chapter XIV
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Descendants of Prithu. Legend of the Prachetasas: they are desired by their father to multiply mankind, by worshipping Vishńu: they plunge into the sea, and meditate on and praise him: he appears, and grants their wishes.

sections.title: Book I, chapter XV
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: The world overrun with trees: they are destroyed by the Prachetasas. Soma pacifies them, and gives them Márishá to wife: her story: the daughter of the nymph Pramlochá. Legend of Kańd u. Márishá's former history. Daksha the son of the Prachetasas: his different characters: his sons: his daughters: their marriages and progeny: allusion to Prahláda, his descendant.

sections.title: Book I, chapter XVI
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Inquiries of Maitreya respecting the history of Prahláda.

sections.title: Book I, chapter XVII
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Legend of Prahláda. Hirańyakaśipu, the sovereign of the universe: the gods dispersed or in servitude to him: Prahláda, his son, remains devoted to Vishńu: questioned by his father, he praises Vishńu: Hirańyakaśipu orders him to be put to death, but in vain: his repeated deliverance: he teaches his companions to adore Vishńu.?

sections.title: Book I, chapter XVIII
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Hirańyakaśipu's reiterated attempts to destroy his son: their being always frustrated.

sections.title: Book I, chapter XIX
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Dialogue between Prahláda and his father: he is cast from the top of the palace unhurt: baffles the incantations of Samvara: he is thrown fettered into the sea: he praises Vishńu.

sections.title: Book I, chapter XX
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Vishńu appears to Prahláda. Hirańyakaśipu relents, and is reconciled to his son: he is put to death by Vishńu as the Nrisinha. Prahláda becomes king of the Daityas: his posterity: fruit of hearing his story.

sections.title: Book I, chapter XXI
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Families of the Daityas. Descendants of Kaśyapa by Danu. Children of Kaśyapa by his other wives. Birth of the Márutas, the sons of Diti.

sections.title: Book I, chapter XXII
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Dominion over different provinces of creation assigned to different beings. Universality of Vishńu. Four varieties of spiritual contemplation. Two conditions of spirit. The perceptible attributes of Vishńu types of his imperceptible properties. Vishńu every thing. Merit of hearing the first book of the Vishńu Puráńa.

sections.title: Book II, chapter I
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Descendants of Priyavrata, the eldest son of Swáyambhuva Manu: his ten sons: three adopt a religious life; the others become kings of the seven Dwípas, or isles, of the earth. Agnídhra, king of Jambu-dwípa, divides it into nine portions, which he distributes amongst his sons. Nábhi, king of the south, succeeded by Rishabha; and he by Bharata: India named after him Bhárata: his descendants reign during the Swáyambhuva Manwantara.

sections.title: Book II, chapter II
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Description of the earth. The seven Dwípas and seven seas. Jambu-dwípa. Mount Meru: its extent and boundaries. Extent of Ilávrita. Groves, lakes, and branches of Meru. Cities of the gods. Rivers. The forms of Vishńu worshipped in different Varshas.

sections.title: Book II, chapter III
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Description of Bhárata-varsha: extent: chief mountains: nine divisions: principal rivers and mountains of Bhárata proper: principal nations: superiority over other Varshas, especially as the seat of religious acts. (Topographical lists.)

sections.title: Book II, chapter IV
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Account of kings, divisions, mountains, rivers, and inhabitants of the other Dwípas, viz. Plaksha, Śálmala, Kuśa, Krauncha, Śáka, and Pushkara: of the oceans separating them: of the tides: of the confines of the earth: the Lokáloka mountain. Extent of the whole.

sections.title: Book II, chapter V
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Of the seven regions of Pátála, below the earth. Nárada's praises of Pátála. Account of the serpent Śesha. First teacher of astronomy and astrology.

sections.title: Book II, chapter VI
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Of the different hells or divisions of Naraka, below Pátála: the crimes punished in them respectively: efficacy of expiation: meditation on Vishńu the most effective expiation.

sections.title: Book II, chapter VII
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Extent and situation of the seven spheres, viz. earth, sky, planets, Mahar-loka, Janaloka, Tapo-loka, and Satya-loka. Of the egg of Brahmá, and its elementary envelopes. Of the influence of the energy of Vishńu.

sections.title: Book II, chapter VIII
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Description of the sun: his chariot; its two axles: his horses. The cities of the regents of the cardinal points. The sun's course: nature of his rays: his path along the ecliptic. Length of day and night. Divisions of time: equinoxes and solstices, months, years, the cyclical Yuga, or age of five years. Northern and southern declinations. Saints on the Lokáloka mountain. Celestial paths of the Pitris, gods, Vishńu. Origin of Gangá, and separation, on the top of Meru, into four great rivers.

sections.title: Book II, chapter IX
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Planetary system, under the type of a Śiśumára or porpoise. The earth nourished by the sun. Of rain whilst the sun shines. Of rain from clouds. Rain the support, of vegetation, and thence of animal life. Náráyańa the support of all beings.

sections.title: Book II, chapter X
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Names of the twelve Ádityas. Names of the Rishis, Gandharbhas, Apsarasas, Yakshas, Uragas, and Rákshasas, who attend the chariot of the sun in each month of the year. Their respective functions.

sections.title: Book II, chapter XI
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: The sun distinct from, and supreme over, the attendants on his car: identical with the three Vedas and with Vishńu: his functions.

sections.title: Book II, chapter XII
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Description of the moon: his chariot, horses, and course: fed by the sun: drained periodically of ambrosia by the progenitors and gods. The chariots and horses of the planets: kept in their orbits by aerial chains attached to Dhruva. Typical members of the planetary porpoise. Vásudeva alone real.

sections.title: Book II, chapter XIII
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Legend of Bharata. Bharata abdicates his throne, and becomes an ascetic: cherishes a fawn, and becomes so much attached to it as to neglect his devotions: he dies: his successive births: works in the fields, and is pressed as a palankin-bearer for the Rájá of Sauvíra: rebuked for his awkwardness: his reply: dialogue between him and the king.

sections.title: Book II, chapter XIV
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Dialogue continued. Bharata expounds the nature of existence, the end of life, and the identification of individual with universal spirit.

sections.title: Book II, chapter XV
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Bharata relates the story of Ribhu and Nidágha. The latter, the pupil of the former, becomes a prince, and is visited by his preceptor, who explains to him the principles of unity, and departs.

sections.title: Book II, chapter XVI
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Ribhu returns to his disciple, and perfects him in divine knowledge. The same recommended to the Rájá by Bharata, who thereupon obtains final liberation. Consequences of hearing this legend.

sections.title: Book III, chapter I
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Account of the several Manus and Manwantaras. Swárochisha the second Manu: the divinities, the Indra, the seven Rishis of his period, and his sons. Similar details of Auttami, Támasa, Raivata, Chákshusha, and Vaivaswata. The forms of Vishńu, as the preserver, in each Manwantara. The meaning of Vishńu.

sections.title: Book III, chapter II
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Of the seven future Manus and Manwantaras. Story of Sanjná and Chháyá, wives of the sun. Sávarńi, son of Chháyá, the eighth Manu. His successors, with the divinities, &c. of their respective periods. Appearance of Vishnu in each of the four Yugas.

sections.title: Book III, chapter III
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Division of the Veda into four portions, by a Vyása, in every Dwápara age. List of the twenty-eight Vyásas of the present Manwantara. Meaning of the word Brahma.

sections.title: Book III, chapter IV
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Division of the Veda, in the last Dwápara age, by the Vyása Krishńa Dwaipáyana. Paila made reader of the Rich; Vaiśampáyana of the Yajush; Jaimini of the Shun; and Sumantu of the Atharvan. Súta appointed to teach the historical poems. Origin of the four parts of the Veda. Sanhitás of the Rig-veda.

sections.title: Book III, chapter V
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Divisions of the Yajur-veda. Story of Yájnawalkya: forced to give up what he has learned: picked up by others, forming the Taittiríya-yajush. Yájnawalkya worships the sun, who communicates to him the Vájasneyí-yajush.

sections.title: Book III, chapter VI
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Divisions of the Sáma-veda: of the Atharva-veda. Four Pauráńik Sanhitás. Names of the eighteen Puráńas. Branches of knowledge. Classes of Rishis.

sections.title: Book III, chapter VII
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: By what means men are exempted from the authority of Yama, as narrated by Bhíshma to Nakula. Dialogue between Yama and one of his attendants. Worshippers of Vishńu not subject to Yama. How they are to be known.

sections.title: Book III, chapter VIII
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: How Vishńu is to be worshipped, as related by Aurva to Sagara. Duties of the four castes, severally and in common: also in time of distress.

sections.title: Book III, chapter IX
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Duties of the religious student, householder, hermit, and mendicant.

sections.title: Book III, chapter X
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Ceremonies to be observed at the birth and naming of a child. of marrying, or leading a religious life. Choice of a wife. Different modes of marrying.

sections.title: Book III, chapter XI
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Of the Sadácháras, or perpetual obligations of a householder. Daily purifications, ablutions, libations, and oblations: hospitality: obsequial rites: ceremonies to be observed at meals, at morning and evening worship, and on going to rest.

sections.title: Book III, chapter XII
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Miscellaneous obligations--purificatory, ceremonial, and moral.

sections.title: Book III, chapter XIII
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Of Śráddhas, or rites in honour of ancestors, to be performed on occasions of rejoicing. Obsequial ceremonies. Of the Ekoddisht a or monthly Śráddha, and the Sapińd ana or annual one. By whom to be performed.

sections.title: Book III, chapter XIV
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Of occasional Śráddhas, or obsequial ceremonies: when most efficacious, and at what places.

sections.title: Book III, chapter XV
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: What Brahmans are to be entertained at Śráddhas. Different prayers to be recited. Offerings of food to be presented to deceased ancestors.

sections.title: Book III, chapter XVI
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Things proper to be offered as food to deceased ancestors: prohibited things. Circumstances vitiating a Śráddha: how to be avoided. Song of the Pitris, or progenitors, heard by Ikshwáku.

sections.title: Book III, chapter XVII
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Of heretics, or those who reject the authority of the Vedas: their origin, as described by Vaśisht ha to Bhíshma: the gods, defeated by the Daityas, praise Vishńu: an illusory being, or Buddha, produced from his body.

sections.title: Book III, chapter XVIII
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Buddha goes to the earth, and teaches the Daityas to contemn the Vedas: his sceptical doctrines: his prohibition of animal sacrifices. Meaning of the term Bauddha. Jainas and Bauddhas; their tenets. The Daityas lose their power, and are overcome by the gods. Meaning of the term Nagna. Consequences of neglect of duty. Story of Śatadhanu and his wife Śaivyá. Communion with heretics to be shunned.

sections.title: Book IV, chapter I
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Dynasties of kings. Origin of the solar dynasty from Brahmá. Sons of the Manu Vaivaswata. Transformations of Ilá or Sudyumna. Descendants of the sons of Vaivaswat; those of Nedisht ha. Greatness of Marutta. Kings of Vaiśálí. Descendants of Śaryáti. Legend of Raivata; his daughter Revatí married to Balaráma.

sections.title: Book IV, chapter II
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Dispersion of Revata's descendants: those of Dhrisht a: those of Nábhága. Birth of Ikshwáku, the son of Vaivaswata: his sons. Line of Vikukshi. Legend of Kakutstha; of Dhundhumára; of Yuvanáśwa; of Mándhátri: his daughters married to Saubhari.

sections.title: Book IV, chapter III
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Saubhari and his wives adopt an ascetic life. Descendants of Mándhátri. Legend of Narmadá and Purukutsa. Legend of Triśanku. Báhu driven from his kingdom by the Haihayas and Tálajanghas. Birth of Sagara: he conquers the barbarians, imposes upon them distinguishing usages, and excludes them from offerings to fire, and the study of the Vedas.

sections.title: Book IV, chapter IV
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: The progeny of Sagara: their wickedness: he performs an Aśwamedha: the horse stolen by Kapila: found by Sagara's sons, who are all destroyed by the sage: the horse recovered by Anśumat: his descendants. Legend of Mitrasaha or Kalmáshapáda, the son of Sudása. Legend of Khat wánga. Birth of Ráma and the other sons of Daśaratha. Epitome of the history of Ráma: his descendants, and those of his brothers. Line of Kuśa. Vrihadbala, the last, killed in the great war.

sections.title: Book IV, chapter V
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Kings of Mithilá. Legend of Nimi, the son of Ikshwáku. Birth of Janaka. Sacrifice of Síradhwaja. Origin of Sítá. Descendants of Kuśadhwaja. Kriti the last of the Maithila princes.

sections.title: Book IV, chapter VI
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Kings of the lunar dynasty. Origin of Soma, or the moon: he carries off Tárá, the wife of Vrihaspati: war between the gods and Asuras in consequence: appeased by Brahmá. Birth of Budha: married to Ilá, daughter of Vaivaswata. Legend of his son Pururavas, and the nymph Urvaśí: the former institutes offerings with fire: ascends to the sphere of the Gandharbas.

sections.title: Book IV, chapter VII
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Sons of Purúravas. Descendants of Amávasu. Indra born as Gádhí. Legend of Richíka and Satyavatí. Birth of Jamadagni and Viśwámitra. Paraśuráma the son of the former. (Legend of Paraśuráma.) Sunahśephas and others the sons of Viśwámitra, forming the Kauśika race.

sections.title: Book IV, chapter VIII
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Sons of Áyus. Line of Kshatravriddha, or kings of Káśí. Former birth of Dhanwantarí. Various names of Pratarddana. Greatness of Alarka.

sections.title: Book IV, chapter IX
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Descendants of Raji, son of Áyus: Indra resigns his throne to him: claimed after his death by his sons, who apostatize from the religion of the Vedas, and are destroyed by Indra. Descendants of Pratíkshatra, son of Kshatravriddha.

sections.title: Book IV, chapter X
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: The sons of Nahusha. The sons of Yayáti: he is cursed by Śukra: wishes his sons to exchange their vigour for his infirmities. Puru alone consents. Yayáti restores him his youth: divides the earth amongst his sons, under the supremacy of Puru.

sections.title: Book IV, chapter XI
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: The Yádava race, or descendants of Yadu. Kárttavírya obtains a boon from Dattátreya: takes Rávańa prisoner: is killed by Paraśuráma: his descendants.

sections.title: Book IV, chapter XII
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Descendants of Krosht ri. Jyámagha's connubial affection for his wife Śaivyá: their descendants kings of Vidarbha and Chedi.

sections.title: Book IV, chapter XIII
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Sons of Satwata. Bhoja princes of Mrittikávatí. Súrya the friend of Satrájit: appears to him in a bodily form: gives him the Syamantaka gem: its brilliance and marvellous properties. Satrájit gives it to Prasena, who is killed by a lion: the lion killed by the bear Jámbavat. Krishńa suspected of killing Prasena, goes to look for him in the forests: traces the bear to his cave: fights with him for the jewel: the contest prolonged: supposed by his companions to be slain: he overthrows Jámbavat, and marries his daughter Jámbavatí: returns with her and the jewel to Dwáraká: restores the jewel to Satrájit, and marries his daughter Satyabhámá. Satrájit murdered by Śatadhanwan: avenged by Krishńa.

sections.title: Book IV, chapter XIV
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Descendants of Śini, of Anamitra, of Śwaphalka and Chitraka, of Andhaka. The children of Devaka and Ugrasena. The descendants of Bhajamána. Children of Śúra: his son Vasudeva: his daughter Prithá married to Páńd u: her children Yudhisht hira and his brothers; also Karńa by Áditya. The sons of Páńd u by Mádrí. Husbands and children of Śúra's other daughters. Previous births of Śiśupála.

sections.title: Book IV, chapter XV
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Explanation of the reason why Śiśupála in his previous births as Hirańyakaśipu and Rávańa was not identified with Vishńu on being slain by him, and was so identified when killed as Śiśupála. The wives of Vasudeva: his children: Balaráma and Krishńa his sons by Devakí: born apparently of Rohińí and Yasodá. The wives and children of Krishńa. Multitude of the descendants of Yadu.

sections.title: Book IV, chapter XVI
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Descendants of Turvasu.

sections.title: Book IV, chapter XVII
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Descendants of Druhyu.

sections.title: Book IV, chapter XVIII
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Descendants of Anu. Countries and towns named after some of them, as Anga, Banga, and others.

sections.title: Book IV, chapter XIX
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Descendants of Puru. Birth of Bharata, the son of Dushyanta: his sons killed: adopts Bharadwája or Vitatha. Hastin, founder of Hastinapur. Sons of Ajámíd ha, and the races derived from them, as Pánchálas, &c. Kripa and Kripí found by Śántanu. Descendants of Riksha, the son of Ajámíd ha. Kurukshetra named from Kuru. Jarásandha and others, kings of Magadhá.

sections.title: Book IV, chapter XX
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Descendants of Kuru. Devápi abdicates the throne: assumed by Śántanu: he is confirmed by the Brahmans: Bhíshma his son by Gangá: his other sons. Birth of Dhritarásht ra, Páńd u, and Vidura. The hundred sons of Dhritarásht ra. The five sons of Páńd u: married to Draupadí: their posterity. Paríkshit, the grandson of Arjuna, the reigning king.

sections.title: Book IV, chapter XXI
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Future kings. Descendants of Paríkshit, ending with Kshemaka.

sections.title: Book IV, chapter XXII
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Future kings of the family of Ikshwáku, ending with Sumitra.

sections.title: Book IV, chapter XXIII
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Future kings of Magadhá: descendants of Vrihadratha.

sections.title: Book IV, chapter XXIV
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Future kings of Magadhá. Five princes of the line of Pradyota. Ten Śaiśunágas. Nine Nandas. Ten Mauryas. Ten Śungas. Four Kańwas. Thirty Ándhrabhrityas. Kings of various tribes and castes, and periods of their rule. Ascendancy of barbarians. Different races in different regions. Period of universal iniquity and decay. Coming of Vishńu as Kalki. Destruction of the wicked, and restoration of the practices of the Vedas. End of the Kali, and return of the Krita, age. Duration of the Kali. Verses chanted by Earth, and communicated by Asita to Janaka. End of the fourth book.

sections.title: Book V, chapter I
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: The death of Kansa announced. Earth, oppressed by the Daityas, applies to the gods. They accompany her to Vishńu, who promises to give her relief. Kansa imprisons Vasudeva and Devakí. Vishńu's instructions to Yoganidrá.

sections.title: Book V, chapter II
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: The conception of Devakí: her appearance: she is praised by the gods.

sections.title: Book V, chapter III
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Birth of Krishńa: conveyed by Vasudeva to Mathurá, and exchanged with the new-born daughter of Yaśodá. Kansa attempts to destroy the latter, who becomes Yoganidrá.

sections.title: Book V, chapter IV
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Kansa addresses his friends, announces their danger, and orders male children to be put to death.

sections.title: Book V, chapter V
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Nanda returns with the infants Krishńa and Balaráma to Gokula. Pútaná killed by the former. Prayers of Nanda and Yaśodá.

sections.title: Book V, chapter VI
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Krishńa overturns a waggon; casts down two trees. The Gopas depart to Vrindávana. Sports of the boys. Description of the season of the rains.

sections.title: Book V, chapter VII
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Krishńa combats the serpent Kálíya: alarm of his parents and companions: he overcomes the serpent, and is propitiated by him: commands him to depart from the Yamuná river to the ocean.

sections.title: Book V, chapter VIII
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: The demon Dhenuka destroyed by Ráma.

sections.title: Book V, chapter IX
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Sports of the boys in the forest. Pralamba the Asura comes amongst them: is destroyed by Ráma, at the command of Krishńa.

sections.title: Book V, chapter X
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Description of autumn. Krishńa dissuades Nanda from worshipping Indra: recommends him and the Gopas to worship cattle and the mountains.

sections.title: Book V, chapter XI
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Indra, offended by the loss of his offerings, causes heavy rain to deluge Gokula. Krishńa holds up the mountain Govarddhana to shelter the cowherds and their cattle.

sections.title: Book V, chapter XII
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Indra comes to Gokula: praises Krishńa, and makes him prince over the cattle. Krishńa promises to befriend Arjuna.

sections.title: Book V, chapter XIII
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Krishńa praised by the cowherds: his sports with the Gopís: their imitation and love of hire. The Rása dance.

sections.title: Book V, chapter XIV
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Krishńa kills the demon Arisht a, in the form of a bull.

sections.title: Book V, chapter XV
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Kansa informed by Nárada of the existence of Krishńa and Balaráma: he sends Keśin to destroy them, and Akrúra to bring them to Mathurá.

sections.title: Book V, chapter XVI
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Keśin, in the form of a horse, slain by Krishńa: he is praised by Nárada.

sections.title: Book V, chapter XVII
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Akrúra's meditations on Krishńa: his arrival at Gokula: his delight at seeing Krishńa and his brother.

sections.title: Book V, chapter XVIII
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Grief of the Gopís on the departure of Krishńa and Balaráma with Akrúra: their leaving Gokula. Akrúra bathes in the Yamuná; beholds the divine forms of the two youths, and praises Vishńu.

sections.title: Book V, chapter XIX
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Akrúra conveys Krishńa and Ráma near to Mathurá, and leaves them: they enter the town. Insolence of Kansa's washerman: Krishńa kills him. Civility of a flower-seller: Krishńa gives him his benediction.

sections.title: Book V, chapter XX
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Krishńa and Balaráma meet Kubjá; she is made straight by the former: they proceed to the palace. Krishńa breaks a bow intended for a trial of arms. Kansa's orders to his servants. Public games. Krishńa and his brother enter the arena: the former wrestles with Cháńúra, the latter with Musht ika, the king's wrestlers; who are both killed. Krishńa attacks and slays Kansa: he and Balaráma do homage to Vasudeva and Devakí: the former praises Krishńa.

sections.title: Book V, chapter XXI
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Krishńa encourages his parents; places Ugrasena on the throne; becomes the pupil of Sándípani, whose son he recovers from the sea: he kills the marine demon Panchajana, and makes a horn of his shell.

sections.title: Book V, chapter XXII
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Jarásandha besieges Mathurá; is defeated, but repeatedly renews the attack.

sections.title: Book V, chapter XXIII
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Birth of Kálayavana: he advances against Mathurá. Krishńa builds Dwáraká, and sends thither the Yádava tribe: he leads Kálayavana into the cave of Muchukunda: the latter awakes, consumes the Yavana king, and praises Krishńa.

sections.title: Book V, chapter XXIV
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Muchukunda goes to perform penance. Krishńa takes the army and treasures of Kálayavana, and repairs with them to Dwáraká. Balaráma visits Vraja: inquiries of its inhabitants after Krishńa.

sections.title: Book V, chapter XXV
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Balaráma finds wine in the hollow of a tree; becomes inebriated; commands the Yamuná to come to him, and on her refusal drags her out of her course: Lakshmí gives him ornaments and a dress: he returns to Dwáraká, and marries Revatí.

sections.title: Book V, chapter XXVI
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Krishńa carries off Rukminí: the princes who come to rescue her repulsed by Balaráma. Rukmin overthrown, but spared by Krishńa, founds Bhojakat a. Pradyumna born of Rukminí.

sections.title: Book V, chapter XXVII
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Pradyumna stolen by Sambara; thrown into the sea, and swallowed by a fish; found by Máyádeví: he kills Sambara, marries Máyádeví, and returns with her to Dwáraká. Joy of Rukminí and Krishńa.

sections.title: Book V, chapter XXVIII
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Wives of Krishńa. Pradyumna has Aniruddha: nuptials of the latter. Balaráma beat at dice, becomes incensed, and slays Rukmin and others.

sections.title: Book V, chapter XXIX
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Indra comes to Dwáraká, and reports to Krishńa the tyranny of Naraka. Krishńa goes to his city, and puts him to death. Earth gives the earrings of Adití to Krishńa, and praises him. He liberates the princesses made captive by Naraka, sends them to Dwáraká, and goes to Swarga with Satyabhámá.

sections.title: Book V, chapter XXX
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Krishńa restores her earrings to Adití, and is praised by her: he visits the gardens of Indra, and at the desire of Satyabhámá carries off the Párijáta tree. Śachí excites Indra to its rescue. Conflict between the gods and Krishńa, who defeats them. Satyabhámá derides them. They praise Krishńa.

sections.title: Book V, chapter XXXI
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Krishńa, with Indra's consent, takes the Párijáta tree to Dwáraká; marries the princesses rescued from Naraka.

sections.title: Book V, chapter XXXII
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Children of Krishńa. Ushá, the daughter of Báńa, sees Aniruddha in a dream, and becomes enamoured of him.

sections.title: Book V, chapter XXXIII
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Báńa solicits Śiva for war: finds Aniruddha in the palace, and makes him prisoner. Krishńa, Balaráma, and Pradyumna come to his rescue Śiva and Skanda aid Báńa: the former is disabled; the latter put to flight. Báńa encounters Krishńa, who cuts off all his arms, and is about to put him to death. Śiva intercedes, and Krishńa a spares his life. Vishńu and Śiva are the same.

sections.title: Book V, chapter XXXIV
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Pauńd raka, a Vásudeva, assumes the insignia and style of Krishńa, supported by the king of Káśí. Krishńa marches against, and destroys them. The son of the king sends a magical being against Krishńa: destroyed by his discus, which also sets Benares on fire, and consumes it and its inhabitants.

sections.title: Book V, chapter XXXV
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Śámba carries off the daughter of Duryodhana, but is taken prisoner. Balaráma comes to Hastinápur, and demands his liberation: it is refused: in his wrath he drags the city towards him, to throw it into the river. The Kuru chiefs give up Śámba and his wife.

sections.title: Book V, chapter XXXVI
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: The Asura Dwivida, in the form of an ape, destroyed by Balaráma.

sections.title: Book V, chapter XXXVII
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Destruction of the Yádavas. Śámba and others deceive and ridicule the Rishis. The former bears an iron pestle: it is broken, and thrown into the sea. The Yádavas go to Prabhása by desire of Krishńa: they quarrel and fight, and all perish. The great serpent Śesha issues from the mouth of Ráma. Krishńa is shot by a hunter, and again becomes one with universal spirit.

sections.title: Book V, chapter XXXVIII
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Arjuna comes to Dwáraká, and burns the dead, and takes away the surviving inhabitants. Commencement of the Kali age. Shepherds and thieves attack Arjuna, and carry off the women and wealth. Arjuna regrets the loss of his prowess to Vyása; who consoles him, and tells him the story of Asht ávakra's cursing the Apsarasas. Arjuna and his brothers place Paríkshit on the throne, and go to the forests. End of the fifth book.

sections.title: Book VI, chapter I
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Of the dissolution of the world: the four ages: the decline of all things, and deterioration of mankind, in the Kali age.

sections.title: Book VI, chapter II
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Redeeming properties of the Kali age. Devotion to Vishńu sufficient to salvation in that age for all castes and persons.

sections.title: Book VI, chapter III
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Three different kinds of dissolution. Duration of a Parárddha. The Clepsydra, or vessel for measuring time. The dissolution that occurs at the end of a day of Brahmá.

sections.title: Book VI, chapter IV
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Continuation of the account of the first kind of dissolution. Of the second kind, or elemental dissolution; of all being resolved into primary spirit.

sections.title: Book VI, chapter V
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: The third kind of dissolution, or final liberation from existence. Evils of worldly life. Sufferings in infancy, manhood, old age. Pains of hell. Imperfect felicity of heaven. Exemption from birth desirable by the wise. The nature of spirit or god. Meaning of the terms Bhagavat and Vásudeva.

sections.title: Book VI, chapter VI
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Means of attaining liberation. Anecdotes of Kháńd ikya and Keśidhwaja. The former instructs the latter how to atone for permitting the death of a cow. Keśidhwaja offers him a requital, and he desires to be instructed in spiritual knowledge.

sections.title: Book VI, chapter VII
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Keśidhwaja describes the nature of ignorance, and the benefits of the Yoga, or contemplative devotion. Of the novice and the adept in the performance of the Yoga. How it is performed. The first stage, proficiency in acts of restraint and moral duty: the second, particular mode of sitting: the third, Pránáyáma, modes of breathing: the fourth, Pratyáhára, restraint of thought: the fifth, apprehension of spirit: the sixth, retention of the idea. Meditation on the individual and universal forms of Vishńu. Acquirement of knowledge. Final liberation.

sections.title: Book VI, chapter VIII
sections.note: Wilson’s chapter heading: Conclusion of the dialogue between Paráśara and Maitreya. Recapitulation of the contents of the Vishńu Puráńa: merit of hearing it: how handed down. Praises of Vishńu. Concluding prayer.

disagreements.title: Life billions of years ago or first initiated 550 million years ago?
disagreements.leftClaim: Strelley Pool’s approximately 3.43-billion-year-old stromatolites are studied as evidence of microbial life.
disagreements.rightClaim: Urantia 58:4.1–2 describes the initiation of the planet’s original life patterns 550 million years ago.
disagreements.incompatibility: If the older structures record terrestrial life, then the first terrestrial life cannot have begun only 550 million years ago.
disagreements.qualification: This comparison depends on the biological interpretation and dating of the structures, and on reading Urantia’s original life patterns as the first life on the same physical Earth.

disagreements.title: Material cosmic development before the scientific early universe?
disagreements.leftClaim: NASA places the early hot universe around 13.8 billion years ago, with stars and galaxies forming later.
disagreements.rightClaim: Urantia 57:1.3 places conditions for a nebular materialization roughly 987 billion years ago.
disagreements.incompatibility: In a shared physical chronology, the described material nebular development cannot predate the early hot universe from which its matter develops.
disagreements.qualification: This comparison assumes both accounts refer to the same physical cosmos and terrestrial year unit. A metaphysical reinterpretation changes what is being claimed.

disagreements.title: A worldwide flood or regional inundations?
disagreements.leftClaim: Genesis 7:19–23 describes waters covering all high mountains and the destruction of land life outside the ark.
disagreements.rightClaim: Urantia 78:7 rejects a worldwide deluge and describes regional Mesopotamian floods.
disagreements.incompatibility: A literal worldwide reading and an explicit denial of worldwide coverage cannot both describe the same physical flood accurately.
disagreements.qualification: This conflict depends on reading Genesis’s universal language literally. Local or literary readings alter the comparison.

quests.question: What exactly did Randall Carlson claim about Halloween, remembrance of the dead and catastrophe, and can that claim withstand comparison?
quests.findings: The submitted brief is the current source of the attribution; an original recording and timestamp are needed. Keep Carlson, Plato, Genesis and geology as four separate viewpoints. Plato’s illustrative 9600 BCE is roughly 11,600 years ago, not 9,600 years ago. Younger Dryas onset, its end and Meltwater Pulse 1B require separate dated records; proximity would not establish a single event.
nextSteps: Find Carlson’s original recording and exact wording.
Test the asserted global date and meaning against independent holiday histories.
Compare dated geological records and uncertainties, distinguishing BP, b2k, BCE and elapsed years.
Do not assign Genesis’s flood a date from another source.

glossary.title: Eridu and Enki/Ea
glossary.description: A Mesopotamian city and its associated deity. Similar names in modern narratives require borrowing checks.

glossary.title: Atlantis
glossary.description: An island civilization in Plato’s Timaeus and Critias, later reinterpreted by spiritual traditions and alternative researchers. Project Timeline compares those accounts without treating their chronologies as equivalent evidence.

glossary.title: Ancient civilizations
glossary.description: A starting point for exploring early settlements, ritual sites, and societies. “Civilization” has different meanings across the sources; each entry should explain the definition it uses.

glossary.title: Flood narratives
glossary.description: Stories about destructive waters appear in many traditions. Similar themes do not, on their own, establish a shared event or a common calendar date.

glossary.title: Göbekli Tepe
glossary.description: A Neolithic site in present-day Türkiye with monumental enclosures and carved pillars. Its UNESCO listing provides an archaeological chronology for the site.

glossary.title: Graham Hancock
glossary.description: Author of Fingerprints of the Gods, Magicians of the Gods, and America Before. Project Timeline indexes his official book synopses separately from archaeological site records; page-level print-edition research remains open.

glossary.title: Randall Carlson
glossary.description: A researcher followed by the project for catastrophe and ancient-landscape topics. The catalog includes a discovery record for Kosmographia episode 024; timestamp-level analysis is still pending.

glossary.title: Plato
glossary.description: The author of Timaeus and Critias. His dialogues provide the classical source for the Atlantis narrative. Stephanus numbers identify passages across editions.

glossary.title: The Bible
glossary.description: A collection of sacred texts interpreted through many religious and historical traditions. Project Timeline distinguishes what a passage says from dates assigned by later interpreters.

glossary.title: The Urantia Book
glossary.description: A spiritual text organized into numbered papers, sections, and paragraphs. Its narratives are presented as claims of the text, with passage-level references.

glossary.title: The Law of One
glossary.description: A body of channeled question-and-answer material also known as the Ra contact. Dates expressed as “years ago” are anchored to the session year before being placed on the timeline.

glossary.title: Neolithic
glossary.description: A regional archaeological term associated with changes in settlement, food production, and material culture. Its dates differ between places.

glossary.title: Buddhism
glossary.description: A research topic connecting Buddhist monuments, art, and the communities that used them.

glossary.title: Stonehenge
glossary.description: A monument built and altered in several phases. The earthwork and stone settings have distinct dated entries.

glossary.title: Cave art
glossary.description: Paintings and engravings preserved in caves. The age of an image and the date of its modern discovery are different events.

glossary.title: Dates, BP, and calendar years
glossary.description: BCE/CE dates, scientific BP ages, and a source’s “years ago” cannot be interchanged without a stated convention. Project Timeline records the basis of each conversion.

glossary.title: Ancient Egypt
glossary.description: Compare archaeological periodization with references to Egypt in classical, biblical, and alternative accounts.

glossary.title: Pyramids
glossary.description: A shape and architectural category used in different societies. Similar forms do not by themselves establish a shared origin.

glossary.title: Modern history
glossary.description: Documents and recorded milestones provide later reference points on the shared time scale.

glossary.title: Creation accounts
glossary.description: Narratives and philosophical accounts of origins. A cosmological story need not supply a calendar date.

glossary.title: Eden
glossary.description: The garden in Genesis and its reinterpretation in the Urantia Book. Each text has its own geography and chronology.

glossary.title: Human origins
glossary.description: A comparison topic for accounts of humanity’s beginnings, ancestry, and migrations. Source categories remain visible.

glossary.title: Nephilim
glossary.description: A term in Genesis 6:4 whose interpretation varies. The indexed entry links directly to the brief passage.

glossary.title: Babel
glossary.description: The city and tower in Genesis 11, associated in the narrative with dispersed languages and peoples.

glossary.title: Abraham / Abram
glossary.description: A central figure in Genesis. Related entries separate individual episodes and compare Melchizedek traditions.

glossary.title: Melchizedek
glossary.description: The king of Salem in Genesis 14 and a figure developed extensively in Urantia Paper 93.

glossary.title: Catastrophe narratives and hypotheses
glossary.description: A comparison topic for destructive floods, fires, and proposed ancient disasters. Shared themes and shared causes are separate questions.

glossary.title: Jesus
glossary.description: Compare canonical Gospel episodes with the additional narrative and explicit dates in the Urantia Book.

glossary.title: Nativity accounts
glossary.description: Accounts of Jesus’s birth and infancy. The texts vary in narrative detail and chronological specificity.

glossary.title: John the Baptist
glossary.description: A figure associated with baptism and the beginnings of Jesus’s ministry; Urantia also gives an infancy chronology.

glossary.title: Crucifixion of Jesus
glossary.description: The execution narrated in the Gospels and associated with later Christian cross symbolism.

glossary.title: Resurrection accounts
glossary.description: Narratives concerning Jesus after the crucifixion, indexed according to the text that presents them.

glossary.title: Pentecost in Acts
glossary.description: The gathering and arrival of the Spirit narrated in Acts 2, followed by an account of the early community.

glossary.title: Manuscripts and editions
glossary.description: A surviving manuscript’s production, its discovery, and a printed edition’s publication belong to separate timelines.

glossary.title: Mesopotamia
glossary.description: The Tigris–Euphrates region supplies geographical context for Sumer, Babel, and several flood interpretations.

glossary.title: Lemuria / Mu
glossary.description: Names used in alternative and channeled accounts of a proposed lost land. The Ra entries retain the dates and terminology of individual sessions.

glossary.title: Cycles of time
glossary.description: Recurring periods play different roles in philosophical and spiritual texts. Numerical cycles here are attributed to their sources.

glossary.title: Younger Dryas
glossary.description: A late-glacial climate interval that is also invoked in alternative catastrophe arguments. The existence of the interval and a proposed impact cause are distinct propositions.

glossary.title: Ignatius Donnelly
glossary.description: Author of Atlantis: The Antediluvian World. Its chapter-level entries document his arguments as an influential alternative interpretation.

glossary.title: Cosmology
glossary.description: Accounts of the universe’s origin and order, including Plato’s philosophical account and spiritual source traditions.

glossary.title: Indus region and Harappan cities
glossary.description: Explore Harappan urban sites alongside later cities in the wider Indus region. Taxila’s later settlements are not assigned to the Harappan civilization.

glossary.title: Water management
glossary.description: Reservoirs, canals, and related infrastructure offer a way to compare how settlements organized water access across different environments.

glossary.title: African kingdoms and urban centers
glossary.description: An index connecting Kush, Aksum, Mapungubwe, and other African political and urban histories. Each place keeps its own chronology.

glossary.title: Trade and exchange networks
glossary.description: Compare the movement of goods, people, and knowledge across linked cities and regions. A shared topic does not prove direct contact between two sites.

glossary.title: Christian traditions
glossary.description: A topic for Christian texts, communities, monuments, and material culture, connected with the separate Symbol Encyclopedia.

glossary.title: Sacred architecture and furnishings
glossary.description: A comparison category for built places of worship and the ritual objects described or used within them. Textual instructions and surviving buildings are different kinds of evidence.

glossary.title: Islamic learning and monuments
glossary.description: Explore the mosques, scholarly institutions, and urban contexts represented in the collection’s African site records.

glossary.title: Mississippian culture
glossary.description: The collection begins this regional topic with Cahokia’s settlements, earthworks, and ceremonial landscape.

glossary.title: Monumental earthworks
glossary.description: Large constructions formed by moving and shaping earth. Poverty Point and Cahokia provide distinct examples with different dates and cultural contexts.

glossary.title: Pueblo histories and places
glossary.description: Explore ancestral settlements and continuing Pueblo communities through Chaco, Mesa Verde, Taos, and related regional records.

glossary.title: Maya cities
glossary.description: Palenque, Tikal, and Copán provide entry points into Maya urban and monumental histories. Their individual site chronologies should not be collapsed into one rise-and-fall date.

glossary.title: Andean societies
glossary.description: A regional index connecting the distinct societies and landscapes represented by Tiwanaku, Chan Chan, and Nasca.

glossary.title: Geoglyphs
glossary.description: Large ground designs. The Nasca and Palpa entry records a particular landscape and date range rather than a universal explanation for such forms.

glossary.title: Exodus
glossary.description: The biblical narrative of departure from Egypt, wilderness travel, and covenant. Its relative sequence is indexed without imposing a disputed BCE chronology.

glossary.title: Moses
glossary.description: The central figure in Exodus’s accounts of deliverance, lawgiving, and sanctuary construction. Entries identify the individual episodes and their passages.

glossary.title: Passover in Exodus
glossary.description: Ritual instructions and a departure narrative in Exodus 12. The entry concerns this textual account; later practices need their own sources.

glossary.title: Sinai in Exodus
glossary.description: The mountain setting of encounter and covenant in Exodus. Project Timeline does not identify a modern archaeological location from the narrative alone.

glossary.title: Covenant in Exodus
glossary.description: The commitments, lawgiving, and renewals described in the Exodus passages indexed here.

glossary.title: Ark of the Covenant
glossary.description: The gold-covered chest specified in Exodus 25. Its description is a textual source, not a claim that the object has been archaeologically identified.

glossary.title: Ice-core chronology
glossary.description: Annual layers and marker horizons allow dated sequences to be compared. The GICC05 records use years before 2000 and retain maximum counting errors.

glossary.title: Ocean circulation and abrupt climate
glossary.description: A research topic linking freshwater routing, Atlantic circulation, and the climate evidence reviewed by NOAA.

glossary.title: Younger Dryas impact hypothesis
glossary.description: A proposed impact explanation for late-glacial changes. The indexed publications include an initial proposal, a critical review, and a bibliographically verified response; this selection is not a complete literature review.

glossary.title: Missoula megafloods
glossary.description: Repeated outburst floods from an ice-dammed lake, studied through regional sediments. Geological megaflood evidence does not itself establish a particular sacred flood narrative or Atlantis claim.

glossary.title: Zecharia Sitchin
glossary.description: Author of the Earth Chronicles. Entries preserve his proposed Anunnaki chronology and distinguish it from archaeological dating.

glossary.title: The Terra Papers
glossary.description: Robert Morning Sky’s attributed narrative of extraterrestrial dynasties and human origins. Available transcription records do not establish the claims as history.

glossary.title: Hindu textual traditions
glossary.description: Distinct sacred texts with different narrative sequences and cyclical time systems. The Vishnu Purana and Satapatha Brahmana are identified separately.

glossary.title: Jan Val Ellam
glossary.description: Author of the Terra Atlantis trilogy. Current entries draw on the official Portuguese book synopses; full chapter coverage remains pending.

symbols.title: Christian / Latin cross
symbols.description: A cross with a longer lower arm. Cultural and historical usage will be documented by era.

historicalUsage.era: Sixth century CE; this object includes modern restoration
historicalUsage.region: Syria · attributed to Antioch or Kaper Koraon
historicalUsage.meaning: A silver cross used in church processions or display, bearing a hymn and a donor inscription.

symbols.title: Templar cross
symbols.description: A starting entry for crosses associated with the Knights Templar. Forms and attributions require artifact-specific research; this glyph is illustrative.

symbols.title: Greek cross
symbols.description: A cross with four equal arms.

symbols.title: Saint Andrew’s cross
symbols.description: A diagonal cross, also called a saltire.

symbols.title: Tau cross
symbols.description: A cross shaped like the capital Greek letter tau.

symbols.title: Celtic cross
symbols.description: A ringed cross. The diagram is a simplified reference, not an artifact reproduction.

symbols.title: Orthodox cross
symbols.description: A cross with additional crossbars; regional variants will have separate usage records.

symbols.title: Patriarchal cross
symbols.description: A cross with two horizontal bars.

symbols.title: Jerusalem cross
symbols.description: A central cross and four smaller crosses; the diagram is schematic.

symbols.title: Maltese cross
symbols.description: An eight-pointed cross; distinguish it from the many forms grouped under “Templar cross.”

historicalUsage.era: Contemporary use with historical institutional associations
historicalUsage.meaning: The eight points are associated with the Beatitudes; the emblem identifies the Order’s charitable and ceremonial activities.

historicalUsage.meaning: The eight-pointed cross appears on the national side of one- and two-euro coins.

symbols.title: Ankh
symbols.description: A looped cross form. Its usage record is reserved for ancient Egyptian and later contexts.

historicalUsage.era: New Kingdom · this object c. 1396–1386 BCE
historicalUsage.meaning: The looped form serves as a sign of life. This record is anchored to a specific faience object from Thutmose IV’s tomb.

symbols.title: Saint Peter’s cross
symbols.description: An inverted Latin cross. Meaning depends on the community, era, and context.

symbols.title: Swastika
symbols.description: A bent-arm cross with long histories in multiple cultures. Usage records must distinguish religious and cultural contexts from Nazi appropriation and modern extremist use. This entry is educational.
